# Decisions the certified frontier makes and a scalar estimator cannot

<!-- GENERATED by `ZIPPY_REGENERATE=1 sbt --server 'testOnly morkl.DecisionsCheck'`; a verify run fails on drift. -->

Every case below is one symbolic program under a stated input precondition. Its residual alternatives are
produced by the supercompiler under several law tables and unroll depths (`Alternatives`), each
with a typed proof trace that has CLOSED (every law step certified, every unfold/fold mechanized) and a
resource certificate per backend (`CostSem`). The choice is made by `Pareto.select`: admission,
constraints proved by the upper bound, dominance over interval-valued work/alloc/rounds/touch, and the declared
tie rule among incomparable survivors. Every alternative is then RUN on every executor that can run it and the
counted events are printed next to the predicted intervals. Two scalar predictors — fewest residual nodes after
the most rewrites, and output cardinality — are evaluated on the same frontier; a case is DIFFERENTIATED when a
scalar predictor names a different winner and the counted run confirms the certified choice.

Nothing here is timed; no measured performance enters a choice. The machine-readable form is
`proofs/decisions/DECISIONS.tsv` plus one selection certificate per case, each replayed independently by
`scripts/check_selection.py`.

## Cases

### tails-disjoint — n-ary tails

The n-ary tails-union of `s ∪ k` is iterated twice (fusable) beside a loop over `s` with a loop-invariant `tails(k)` (hoistable). With disjoint heads the union of the two inputs is a pointer attach and the tails-union's children are accepted whole; which residual allocates least depends on how many times the merged tails are rebuilt, not on how many paths come out.

**Precondition.** s and k have DISJOINT head sets ({a,b} against {c,d}); every path has length 3

**Objective.** alloc: minimise alloc then work then rounds then touch over reference,trie,graph,zipper.

**Program.** `(TailsUnion((S"s" \/ S"k")).iter(P"h", S"r", (P"h" x (S"r" /\ S"k")) ) \/ (TailsUnion((S"s" \/ S"k")).iter(P"h", S"r", (P"h" x TailsUnion(S"r")) ) \/ S"s".iter(P"h", S"r", ((P"h" x (S"r" \ S"k")) \/ TailsUnion(S"k")) )))`

**Alternatives.** 2 on the frontier (30 pruned, 0 refused); every trace closed, every certificate certified.

### range-after-call — first/last range

A `Range` keeps the first one or two paths of a call's result. An output-cardinality estimator sees one or two paths and calls every alternative cheap; the work is in building the call's result before ranging, and the alternatives differ in how the callee's two loops and its invariant are composed after inlining.

**Precondition.** s has 6 paths over heads {a,b,c}, k has 5; the ranges keep at most 2 and 1 result paths

**Objective.** work: minimise work then alloc then rounds then touch over reference,trie,graph,zipper.

**Program.** `(Range(f(; S"s", S"k"), 0, 2) \/ Range(f(; (S"s" \/ S"k"), S"k"), 0, 1))`

### fusion-alloc-work — fusion

Two same-source loops fuse into one (one pass, one loop entry per head) and an invariant branch hoists out of a third loop. Fusion saves loop entries and dispatches but merges two bodies' allocations; hoisting saves allocation but adds a guard composition. Neither trade is visible to a node count.

**Precondition.** s has 6 paths over heads {a,b,c}, k has 5 paths over {x,y,q,a,b}

**Objective.** alloc: minimise alloc then work then rounds then touch over reference,trie,graph,zipper.

### fusion-work-trie — fusion

The same frontier under the other half of the trade: minimise trie work. Fusing the two loops saves allocation (one accumulator instead of two and a merged wrap per head) but the fused body does more dispatch work per head on the trie; the unfused residual — larger, fewer rewrites — has the tighter work bound and the smaller counted work. A rewrite count picks the fused one.

**Precondition.** the same inputs as fusion-alloc-work; the caller can only run the trie executor

**Objective.** work-on-trie: minimise work then alloc then rounds then touch over trie.

**Program.** `((S"s".iter(P"h", S"r", (P"h" x (S"r" /\ S"k")) ) \/ S"s".iter(P"h", S"r", (P"h" x TailsUnion(S"r")) )) \/ (S"s".iter(P"h", S"r", ((P"h" x (S"r" \ S"k")) \/ S"k") ) \/ ((S"s" \/ TailsUnion(S"k")) <| Literal(SpaceValue("a", "b")))))`

### pointer-rebuild — pointer-preserving rebuild

Restricting a four-way union by two prefixes: pushed to the operands, each restriction accepts or rejects whole subtries by pointer and the small operands are rebuilt cheaply; applied to the materialized union, the union itself is built first. The residuals have different node counts and the smaller one is not the one that allocates less.

**Precondition.** s has 36 paths of length 3 under heads {a,b,c}; k has 3 paths; the restriction prefixes are {a, b.x}

**Objective.** alloc: minimise alloc then work then rounds then touch over reference,trie,graph,zipper.

**Program.** `(((("a" x S"k") \/ S"s") \/ (TailsUnion(S"k") \/ ("b" x S"s"))) <| (Literal(SpaceValue("a")) \/ Literal(SpaceValue("b.x"))))`

### puzzle15-expand — puzzle15 projection/materialization

One BFS expansion of the 15-puzzle on every backend: the board is superposed into per-cell projections, moves are applied, and the result is collapsed back. The materialization choice is `comp-lit-to-wraps`: the literal move table composed with the projected board is either kept as one composition (attached under each move prefix in one pass) or MATERIALISED as a union of wraps, one copy of the projection per literal path. The materialised residual is smaller after more rewrites, and a rewrite count prefers it; keeping the composition does less work, which the certified intervals predict and the counted run confirms. The backends differ in what they materialise (the zipper walks, the trie shares subtries by pointer, the graph runs the operation DAG). Over every backend the graph executor wins and it happens to prefer the materialised residual, so the rewrite count agrees here; the companion case restricts the backend and the agreement ends.

**Precondition.** the frontier is the single initial board (blank at c0, tiles 1..15 in order); one BFS expansion

**Objective.** work: minimise work then alloc then rounds then touch over reference,trie,graph,zipper.

**Program.** `S"frontier".iter(P"q", S"__n0h1563746854", S"__n0h1563746854".iter(P"ft0", S"__n1h1563746854", S"__n1h1563746854".iter(P"ft1", S"__n2h1563746854", S"__n2h1563746854".iter(P"ft2", S"__n3h1563746854", S"__n3h1563746854".iter(P"ft3", S"__n4h1563746854", S"__n4h1563746854".iter(P"ft4", S"__n5h1563746854", S"__n5h1563746854".iter(P"ft5", S"__n6h1563746854", S"__n6h1563746854".iter(P"ft6", S"__n7h156374`

**Alternatives.** 4 on the frontier (2 pruned, 0 refused); every trace closed, every certificate certified.

### puzzle15-expand-reference — puzzle15 projection/materialization

The same four residuals of the 15-puzzle expansion, priced for the reference evaluator only. Here materialising the projection under each move prefix (`comp-lit-to-wraps`) COSTS work — every copy is re-evaluated — so the residual that keeps the composition, larger and reached by fewer rewrites, is the certified choice; the rewrite count picks the materialised one. Which residual is cheaper depends on the backend, which is exactly what a backend-blind heuristic cannot express and a per-backend certificate can.

## What a case does not show

The trie, zipper and graph intervals are the must/may envelopes of the abstract interpretation; they are
sound and often wide, so dominance across backends is rarely provable and the tie rule (least upper bound) decides
among incomparable survivors — the certificate says which survivors overlap the selected one. The reference
evaluator's `touch` has no counted oracle and is never compared. A case marked AGREES is one where the scalar
predictor happened to name the certified choice; it is recorded, not hidden.
